source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Design: within-subjects lab study, three small API-misuse defects from Stack Overflow, each debugged in three timed stages with more resources each time. People wrote down every hypothesis they held at each stage, before they could test it.
numbers: N=20 developers (25 recruited, 5 piloted), 60 debugging sessions. Latin-square assignment of aids to tasks. Stage limits 7, 10 and 20 minutes. Programs 36 to 45 lines. Experience 0-20 years (median 2); tech knowledge 1-8 of 9 (median 4).
limits: Graduate-course sample, tiny programs, no internet. Task 3 had a 90% success rate, so tasks differ in difficulty.
agent_relevance: The staged design is a template for measuring hypothesis quality before testing. We can log the agent's hypotheses at S3 before any S4 check, then score them.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Developers form few hypotheses and most are wrong. Only 11% were correct in stage 1 (symptom only), 25% by stage 2 (code and docs), 39% by stage 3 (can run and edit).
numbers: Control condition, 20 sessions. Stage 1: 27 hypotheses, 3 correct (11%). Stage 2: 35 total, 9 correct (25%). Stage 3: 38 total, 15 correct (39%). Median 2 hypotheses per defect, max 4.
limits: Hypotheses scored correct by keyword match to the Stack Overflow answer. Participants were told to report as many as they could, so the low count is not just low effort.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis generation is the bottleneck, and one sample gives few candidates. The agent should draw many independent hypotheses, not one. Fits S3 GENERATE.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Holding the correct hypothesis by stage 2 predicts final success. A logistic model across all 60 sessions gave about 5 times higher odds of fixing the defect.
numbers: Odds about 5x, p=0.01 (60 sessions, controls: years of experience, tech knowledge, task). 20 of 60 sessions failed to fix. 6 of those 20 had the correct hypothesis at stage 2 but still failed.
limits: Correlational: hypotheses were measured, not randomly assigned in this analysis. A right hypothesis is not enough; 6 sessions still failed.
agent_relevance: A right hypothesis is necessary-ish but not sufficient. S4 TEST and S5 REVISE still matter after a correct hypothesis is found.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Supplying potential hypotheses raised success about six-fold. Supplying fault locations did not help at all.
numbers: Ordinal logistic regression (Table IV): potential hypotheses OR 6.24 (SE 0.88, p=0.03); fault locations OR 1.4 (SE 0.77, p=0.64); years of experience OR 1.14 (p=0.04); tech knowledge OR 2.19 (p=0.07). Text gives p=0.0388 for hypotheses. Table III reads as successes of about 11/20 control, 13/20 fault locations, 16/20 hypotheses (sums to 40/60, matching 20 failures), but the extracted table is garbled so this split is low confidence.
quote: Participants who received potential debugging hypotheses were six times more likely to fix the fault compared to the other groups
limits: Each participant got two hypotheses with test steps, drawn from the true Stack Overflow answer and generalised, so the aid contained the answer; a real generator would not. The exact mix of correct and incorrect items per task is not confirmed (Table II lists both). p only just under 0.05, N=20. No replication found this session.
agent_relevance: Supports a generator-plus-tester design: given plausible candidate causes, a checker can do the rest. Caution: this is an upper bound; measure our own generator's recall of the true cause.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Fault locations (what automated fault localisation gives) did not help people form correct hypotheses or fix the defect. Knowing where without knowing why was not enough.
numbers: Share with a correct hypothesis, fault-location group vs control: stage 2 45% vs 45% (p=0.4125); stage 3 60% vs 75% (p=0.1320). Fix rate not different (p=0.6710).
quote: I looked at the buggy line help, [but] I was still not sure how to fix the code.
limits: Null result with small N, so low power; absence of evidence, not proof of no effect. Locations were given as lines, with no explanation.
agent_relevance: A location without a cause is weak help. A failing line must still be turned into a causal story that S4 can test.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Supplied hypotheses did not make people faster. The gain was in success, not time. People still had to understand the hypothesis and link it to the code.
numbers: No significant difference in median time to success (f=0.51, p=0.61). Share of time reading documentation among successes: 5% control, 17% fault locations, 6% hypotheses (f=1.7, p=0.19).
limits: Time analysed only for successful sessions; small cells.
agent_relevance: Hypotheses buy accuracy, not speed. Spend budget on testing candidates, not on generating more once a few good ones exist (G12).

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Preliminary study: three professional developers on live-streams, with the internet. Without a correct hypothesis they searched blindly and read irrelevant material; a wrong first hypothesis sent them to the wrong documentation. One gave up after about 30 minutes; the real fix, found next day, was an unrelated missing API call.
numbers: N=3 streams (177, 85 and 104 minutes). D1 hypothesised a missing file-type option for the shelve API. D2 first blamed standard I/O. D3 blamed async APIs.
limits: Three cases chosen by the authors; anecdotal.
agent_relevance: Illustrates wrong-hypothesis lock-in and search driven by a bad frame. G1/G2: reframe only on a failed check, and make the check cheap so a wrong hypothesis is dropped fast.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: The background section places debugging hypotheses in program-comprehension theory (Brooks: hypothesis-driven comprehension; Letovsky: conjectures as answers to questions). It says professionals mostly use the 'intuitive method' of forming and testing hypotheses, and that one user study found fault localisation does not always help debugging.
numbers: Cites Brooks, Letovsky, Robin (novice vs expert), Parnin and Orso. No new numbers.
limits: Citation summary, not my own reading of Brooks, Letovsky or Robin.
agent_relevance: Gives the lineage from comprehension theory to debugging hypotheses. The hypothesis is the unit of S3.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2021) An Exploratory Study of Debugging Episodes
finding: Table 1 of the episodes paper lists prior debugging studies with sizes. The hypothesis-era studies were small: Gould 10 participants, Vessey 16, Katz and Anderson 77 (mostly students), Gugerty and Olson 44, Bohme 12, Layman 15. Only five studies watched professionals in the field.
numbers: Table 1 values as listed.
limits: Table copied from the 2021 authors; I did not check each cell against the originals.
agent_relevance: Shows how thin the founding evidence is. Treat classic findings as hypotheses to test on our agent, not facts.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2021) An Exploratory Study of Debugging Episodes
finding: The 2021 authors summarise the field: developers follow a simple hypothesis-testing strategy, guess causes from experience and output clues, then test by editing code or inspecting state. Both forward reasoning (follow the failing run) and backward reasoning (work back from wrong output) are used.
numbers: Cites Perscheid, Gould, Gugerty, Bohme, Katz. No numbers.
limits: Secondary summary.
agent_relevance: Two search directions to offer as operators: trace forward from the input, trace backward from the wrong output.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2021) An Exploratory Study of Debugging Episodes
finding: Naturalistic study of debugging episodes in live-streamed work. Debugging is frequent, no single activity dominates, long episodes use many activities and short episodes are mostly edit-and-test.
numbers: Debugging about once every 8 minutes of programming. Episodes ranged from seconds to over 100 minutes with a skewed distribution; the longest 25% of episodes took most of the debugging time. Dataset more than 100 hours, 33 professionals.
limits: Streamers think aloud and may behave differently from private work. Open-source projects only.
agent_relevance: Most episodes are quick and a minority are long. The budget rule (G12) should expect heavy-tailed difficulty.

source: Alaboudi & LaToza (2021) Edit-Run Behavior in Programming and Debugging
finding: Debugging proceeds as many short edit-run cycles, which the authors link to testing hypotheses by trying a change and running. Developers test several wrong hypotheses before the fix.
numbers: 28 hours, 11 professionals, 581 debugging and 207 programming edit-run cycles. About 7 cycles before fixing a defect. Mean debugging cycle 1 minute vs programming 3 minutes. Cycles with gaps were 4 times longer.
limits: The link from cycle to hypothesis is the authors' interpretation; hypotheses were not coded one by one. Same live-stream data source.
agent_relevance: Testing by trying a change is cheap for people but each agent step costs tokens; prefer a probe or print to a speculative edit when possible.

source: Li & Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Grounded theory from think-aloud sessions in familiar codebases. None of the developers stated a formal testable hypothesis. They held vague speculations, tracked what they knew and did not know, and built a good-enough mental model.
numbers: 7 professionals on 11 tasks (7.8 hours) plus 5 streamers on 6 tasks (3.1 hours). Time spent: 12% reproducing, 57% updating the mental model, 13% fixing, 18% validating (paper states these as averages).
quote: None of the developers articulated formal hypotheses; instead, they voiced casual thoughts about the system
limits: Small sample; interpretive grounded theory; think-aloud may shift behaviour; tasks had to be shareable, so the hardest industry cases may be missing.
agent_relevance: Human practice is looser than scientific-method debugging. The agent may do better by forcing explicit hypotheses with predictions; that is an empirical question (see AutoSD).

source: Li & Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Developers deliberately avoid premature commitment. One listed several speculations but did not check them to avoid jumping to conclusions, and used a structured top-down traversal to update uncertainty. Developers avoid learning more than they must.
numbers: P1 spent 52 minutes finding which change introduced the bug, 12 minutes looking for prior fixes and 13 minutes reproducing at a different scope. Forward tracing dominated in high-familiarity code, backward tracing in low-familiarity and longer tasks (forward used by 7 of 8 participants).
quote: just to try to not to jump to conclusions
limits: One participant's case; small sample.
agent_relevance: A counter to fixation: hold several unchecked candidate causes and gather evidence systematically before committing. Matches G1 while keeping alternatives alive.

source: Li & Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: The paper reports a gap between what developers say and do. Interviews and personal accounts say scientific method; observation shows other strategies (forward reasoning, code reading). A review of 74 papers found 12 strategies. Bohme et al. had 12 engineers fix 27 bugs and saw forward reasoning and code comprehension used most. In a VR performance-bug study, explicit hypothesis testing appeared in only 79 fifteen-second instances vs 832 of source inspection.
numbers: Review of 74 papers: 12 strategies. DbgBench: 12 engineers, 27 bugs. VR study: 12 participants, 79 vs 832 instances.
quote: Hypotheses are known to be valuable; correct hypotheses predict debugging success [3].
limits: Second-hand figures quoted in the paper; in the VR study all participants worked on one bug.
agent_relevance: Self-reports overstate the scientific method. Use observed behaviour as the baseline, not textbook advice.

source: Li & Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Information foraging theory predicts developers follow information scent to guide search rather than test hypotheses. Interviews of 8 professionals reported variants of the scientific method.
numbers: Cites Lawrance and Piorkowski on IFT. A live-stream study found debugging is 41% editing and 29% testing.
limits: Secondary summary.
agent_relevance: A competing explanation to hypothesis-driven theory. The agent can combine both: generate hypotheses, then rank them by scent such as error-text matches.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: AutoSD makes an LLM follow scientific debugging: write a hypothesis, a prediction and a debugger experiment; run it for real; read the observation; conclude supported, rejected or undecided. Rejected hypotheses are removed from the prompt before the patch is written because that improved repair.
numbers: Loop: Hypothesis, Prediction, Experiment, Observation, Conclusion. 10 patches per bug, matching Jiang et al.
quote: Hypothesis: a tentative description that explains the bug and is consistent with the known observations
limits: The scheme is Zeller's scientific debugging; the prompt includes hand-written examples.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S3 to S4 to S5: a hypothesis plus a prediction before the test, and drop rejected hypotheses from context.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Repair results: AutoSD is competitive with a plain LLM baseline and adds explanations. The gain in raw counts is small.
numbers: ARHE: LLM-Base 179 plausible and 177 correct; AutoSD 189 plausible and 187 correct. Defects4J v2.0 plausible counts read as 110 vs 113 from a garbled figure.
limits: Defects4J numbers come from a garbled figure; column mapping uncertain. Possible training-data contamination on Defects4J.
agent_relevance: The structured loop did not cost accuracy and gave a readable trace. Its value is explanation and a confidence signal, not a large accuracy jump.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Real execution matters. If the LLM invents the debugger output, results get worse, and the done signal stops being informative.
numbers: Plausible-patch rate per run 73% with a real debugger vs 63% with hallucinated output. The DONE signal made a plausible patch 12.4 points more likely with real execution but 11 points less likely when hallucinated. Plausible patches with DONE: 89% correct vs 82% without.
limits: Hallucination ablation on ARHE only. Percent-point figures are the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2/G10: an observation must come from code, not from the model. Hypothesis text without a real check can mislead.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Human study: explanations helped on real bugs, but one case shows over-trust.
numbers: N=20 (8 undergraduates, 6 graduates, 6 professionals), 6 patches each in 30-40 minutes, 3 with explanation. Accuracy higher with explanation in 7 of 12 patches (5 of 6 real BugsInPy bugs), lower in 2 (ARHE105, where participants accepted the reasoning without scrutiny; BIP003, where people grew more cautious). 70% wanted explanations; 55% satisfied with the format.
limits: Small N; the task was patch review, not debugging; students dominate the sample.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis trace can persuade a reader that a wrong fix is right. Do not use trace quality as a correctness signal (G10).

source: Zhong et al. (2024) Debug like a Human: LDB, verifying runtime execution step by step
finding: LDB shows the model the actual variable values after each basic block and asks it to judge each block. This beats having the model imagine the trace (self-debugging with explanation or trace) and keeps improving over rounds while self-debug methods stall after 2-3 rounds.
numbers: HumanEval with GPT-3.5 seed 73.8%: Self-Debugging +7.3, LDB +9.1 (82.9%). GPT-4 seed 87.2%: +1.2 vs +2.4. Reflexion seed 91.5%: +0.6 vs +3.6 (95.1%). Claimed gain up to 9.8% overall. 20 rounds reach 84.1% on HumanEval (GPT-3.5). Buggy-block localisation judged correct in over 85% on all sets (95.5% MBPP, 86.7% TransCoder).
limits: Gains shrink as the seed code gets better. Localisation was judged by GPT-4, not by humans. Benchmarks are small functions.
agent_relevance: Again, runtime facts beat model-imagined traces. Block-level verdicts are a cheap hypothesis space: which block is wrong.

source: Arafa, Solomon, Navabpour, Fischmeister (2017) Debugging Behaviour of Embedded-Software Developers
finding: Embedded-software debugging by 14 intermediate programmers. Locating the bug is harder than fixing it. Successful attempts ran the unmodified program first and edited one function per try.
numbers: N=14 students, 7 bugs, 2-hour slots. 93.75% of post-bug forms (30 of 32) rated locating at least as hard as fixing. Successful attempts first ran the program unchanged in 88.9% (16 of 18); 75% (6 of 8) who edited before the first run failed. Mean transitions between activities 43.1 in unsuccessful vs 26.97 in successful attempts.
limits: Students, one RTOS, exploratory, no random assignment; correlations only.
agent_relevance: Observe before editing, in line with G2. Many edits per try signal flailing.

source: Arafa, Solomon, Navabpour, Fischmeister (2017) Debugging Behaviour of Embedded-Software Developers
finding: A fixation-like failure: considering only one cause. On a bug needing two missing lines, 10 of 11 participants located it but only 3 fixed it, because many inserted one line.
numbers: Bug-3: 11 examined, 10 located, 3 fixed.
limits: One bug, small sample; the cause is the authors' reading.
agent_relevance: After a fix passes part of a check, ask whether there are further causes. Supports a G3-type check on a wider test instead of stopping at the first plausible fix.

source: Gould (1975) Some psychological evidence on how people debug computer programs
finding: Gould (1975): 10 experienced programmers debugged the same 12 FORTRAN listings, each with one non-syntactic error. They rarely used the interactive debugging tools that were available. The paper sets out basic concepts and a gross theory of debugging (form hypotheses, then verify), and replicates Gould and Drongowski (1974).
numbers: N=10, 12 listings. Median debug time about 7 minutes; about 11% of listings had the bug not found; fewer than 1 incorrect assertion about the bug location per listing. Assignment-statement bugs about 3 times harder to find than array or interaction bugs. About 3 times more efficient on a program previously debugged with a different bug.
quote: a gross theory of debugging is described
limits: Only the IBM abstract page was read, not the full paper. Fortran listings on paper, 1970s, one-line bugs. DOI 10.1016/S0020-7373(75)80005-8.
agent_relevance: Founding evidence of hypothesise-then-verify as the human norm. Bug type matters: assignment bugs are hard, so difficulty varies by class (G12).

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Vessey (1985): 16 programmers (8 expert, 8 novice) thought aloud while debugging a COBOL program. Expertise was defined by ability to chunk the program, and chunking strongly related to strategy. The paper proposes, for later testing, that experts go breadth-first with a system view and smooth progress, and novices go depth-first and erratically.
numbers: N=16 from one organisation; verbal protocol analysis. The expert and novice strategy statements are propositions, not confirmed results.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; the PDF is a scanned image I could not read. Strategy statements were offered as ideas to test.
agent_relevance: Depth-first on one early hypothesis is the novice pattern; breadth-first (several candidates plus a system view) is the expert pattern. A design rule for S3.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Reported in a search summary only: in Vessey's results experts respond to the data in the task while novices are constrained by preconceived ideas or early hypotheses about the error source.
numbers: Not verified in primary text.
quote: experts respond to the data in the task while novices are constrained by preconceived ideas or early hypotheses
limits: A search-result paraphrase of a secondary description; I did not read the paper's own results.
agent_relevance: The clearest founding statement of fixation on early hypotheses. Check against the original before we cite it as fact.

source: Katz & Anderson (1987) Debugging: an analysis of bug-location strategies
finding: Reported in a secondary review only: students debugging Lisp used three bug-location strategies (heuristic mapping from symptom to origin, hand simulation, causal reasoning). Goal-driven reasoning dominated when debugging their own code; data-driven hand simulation dominated for others' code.
numbers: Not verified. The ETS page gave only the citation (Human-Computer Interaction 3(4), 351-399). Alaboudi 2021 Table 1 lists N=77.
limits: Secondary only. Strategy labels may differ from the original.
agent_relevance: Debugging your own work differs from debugging another's. An agent debugging its own output may lean on goal-driven (hypothesis-first) search; plan a check against self-confirmation.

source: Gilmore (1991) Models of debugging
finding: Reported in a secondary review only: Gilmore argued comprehension is not a separate step before debugging; understanding keeps developing during the debugging loop. Deeper bugs were found more easily, which he took as evidence that bugs are detected during ongoing comprehension. Locating errors involves repeated cycles of hypothesis formation and testing.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Only a search-result description; the exact citation and DOI were not checked. It disagrees with Katz and Anderson's model that assumes full understanding first.
agent_relevance: Supports a loop where the model of the program is updated by each test, not frozen at S1/S2 (S2 REPRESENT may need updating inside the loop).

source: Ko & Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline
finding: Interrogative debugging: ask why-did and why-didn't questions about a failure instead of guessing where to look. In user tests on Alice, the Whyline cut debugging time by nearly 8 times and helped programmers complete 40% more tasks.
numbers: About 8x less debugging time; 40% more tasks completed (abstract figures).
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex). Alice is a teaching environment; small tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports question-driven hypothesis generation: derive candidate causes from why and why-not questions on the wrong output (backward reasoning).

source: Ko & Myers (2009) Finding causes of program output with the Java Whyline
finding: The Java Whyline tested the idea on real open-source bug reports against a breakpoint debugger.
numbers: Whyline users succeeded about 3 times as often and about 2 times as fast. Two real bug reports, controlled experiment.
limits: Abstract only; N not read. Same group as the 2004 tool, so not independent.
agent_relevance: Tools that remove the need to guess where to look help. Guessing where to look is the weak step.

source: Parnin & Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Parnin and Orso ran user studies of automated fault localisation and found that several assumptions of such tools do not hold in practice (for example that seeing a faulty statement in isolation is enough). Consistent with the null effect of fault locations in Alaboudi 2020.
numbers: Two user studies, with and without the tool; N not read here.
limits: Abstract only (OpenAlex). The paper is described as preliminary.
agent_relevance: Do not assume localisation alone solves debugging; keep the causal hypothesis step.

source: Bohme et al. (2017) How developers debug software: the DbgBench dataset
finding: DbgBench: 12 professional engineers spent about a month localising, explaining and fixing 27 real bugs in widely used programs, giving a human gold standard for diagnoses and strategies.
numbers: 12 engineers, 27 bugs, about one month.
limits: Abstract only; not read beyond that.
agent_relevance: A realistic human benchmark of diagnoses, useful for comparing our agent's hypotheses with human explanations.

source: Follow-ups to AutoSD: DoVer (2025), mutation testing via scientific debugging (2025), DebugHarness (2026)
finding: Forward citations carry the hypothesis-test pattern into new settings. DoVer tests failure hypotheses by intervening in multi-agent runs and says log-only debugging yields untested hypotheses. Scientific debugging was reused for mutation-test generation, where iterative refinement mattered. DebugHarness has the agent form hypotheses and probe live memory for security bugs.
numbers: DoVer: flips 18-28% of failed trials to success; validates or refutes 30-60% of hypotheses; recovers 49% on GSMPlus with AG2. DebugHarness: patches about 90% of SEC-bench bugs, over 30% relative gain over baselines. Mutation testing: LLM beats Pynguin on fault detection and coverage at higher cost.
limits: Abstracts only (arXiv API); numbers are the authors' own claims.
agent_relevance: The same lesson across settings: a hypothesis is only useful once tested by action. Fits G2 and G3.
